title: The Pub Fight That Broke a Village
central_question: After the Black Death, a pay rise was a crime and every neighbour was the police. What happened when a pub fight went wrong?
setting: An English village, harvest 1351, three years after the Black Death; the alehouse, the parish church, the road to Dover.
dialogue_note: Narration and dialogue use modern Australian slang on purpose; nobody in 1351 spoke like this.

lines.text: Harvest, 1351, when a pay rise is a crime.
Your best mate's got blood on his hands, and he's bashing on the church door.
Touch him now, and you're in strife. With God.
So how'd a few ales end up here? Rewind twelve hours.

badges.text: You, Jacko, Simmo and this night are fictional

lines.text: Sunup to sundown, it's hard yakka in the lord's wheat.
Three years back, the Black Death killed maybe half of England.
Now there aren't enough hands. And every pair of hands knows it.

cards.title: England, 1351
cards.sub: Harvest · three years after the Black Death

lines.text: Fair dinkum, the lord over the hill's paying double!
That's against the law, you drongo.
He's right. The Statute of Labourers froze pay at the old, pre-plague rates.
Take more, and you could be fined or jailed.
Worse, the extra could go towards the village's tax bill.
So every neighbour has a reason to dob you in.

badges.text: Legal max for reapers: 2d-3d a day
Excess pay went to the village's tax

lines.text: Sundown. Maud's hung the bush out on the ale-stake, so there's a fresh brew.
My shout, boys! On the lord!
Watch Simmo. He's not drinking. He's counting.

badges.text: Ale-stake: a sign that ale was for sale

lines.text: Flashing that money round? I'll dob you in to the justices.
Rack off, you dobbing mongrel!
Pride, ale, and fourteen hours of hard yakka. Short fuse.
Simmo's not getting up.
Your heart's going like the clappers. And there's no police.
The police... were you.
Whoever found a body had to raise the hue and cry, and everyone had to give chase.

badges.text: Hue and cry: a legal duty

lines.text: So you hunt your best mate through the dark, a horn wailing behind you.
Every step, you're praying you don't catch him.
Let a killer get away, and the whole village gets fined.
He makes the church. Sanctuary.
For up to forty days, no one can drag him out. So the neighbours keep watch.
Night after night, you hear your best mate breathing through the door.
Morning. Simmo can't be buried till the king's coroner has seen him.
Who struck the blow? Speak up, lad.
A jury of your neighbours, every eye on you.
Lie for your mate, or tell it straight and he could hang.
Even the jug's on the hook. It's a 'deodand', and Maud has to pay its value.
Jacko confesses, and swears to leave England. Forever.
With his clothes and a wooden cross,
he must walk the king's highway to the port, by a set day.
Usually Dover. One abjurer in 1353 got twelve days.
Stray off the road, and he could be killed.
One blue. One man dead, one exiled, and a village that can't look itself in the eye.
And the labour laws got nastier. By 1361, runaways could be branded on the forehead.
With an F, for 'falsity'.
Twenty years later, the anger exploded: the Peasants' Revolt.
Next time: you become a Roman gladiator.

badges.text: 1361 law; no evidence it was used

claims.text: You, Jacko, Simmo, Maud, the coroner, the village, the dialogue and this night are fictional; the dialogue and narration use modern Australian slang on purpose. The map is not to scale.
The Black Death of 1348-49 killed perhaps around half of England's people; estimates run from about a third to 60% or more and historians still disagree.
The Statute of Labourers (1351), following the Ordinance of 1349, pinned wages to the customary rates of 1346-47 or the years just before the plague, and obliged the able-bodied to work.
The 1351 statute's maximum for reapers was 2d a day in the first week of August and 3d in the second, without food or drink (translation).
Excess wages taken against the statutes were to be paid towards the township's share of the king's tax (the tenth and fifteenth), giving taxpayers an interest in enforcement.
Taking or paying wages above the legal rate could bring fines, forfeiture of the excess and imprisonment; enforcement was uneven.
A statute of 1361 (34 Edw. III c.10) authorised branding runaway labourers on the forehead with an F 'for the falsity'; there is no evidence it was actually carried out.
Everyone who heard the hue and cry had to follow it; villages that failed to pursue or capture offenders were fined (e.g. Oxford 1285, Kent 1241).
A sudden death had to be viewed by the coroner with a jury drawn from neighbouring vills; the first finder raised the hue; burying a body before the coroner's view was punished.
An object that caused a death was a deodand: the jury valued it and its owner paid that value, in theory for pious uses, in practice usually to the Crown.

A felon could take sanctuary in a church for up to 40 days, then confess to the coroner and abjure the realm: assigned a port (most often Dover), a set number of days, and the king's highway, carrying a wooden cross and stripped of goods but his clothes. Leaving the highway made him liable to be killed. In Norfolk in 1353 an abjurer was given 12 days to leave from Dover.
Neighbours kept watch on the church so that a fugitive in sanctuary could not escape, and could be fined if he did (weaker attribution).
Women brewed and sold most village ale; an ale-stake, a pole often with a bush, showed that ale was for sale.
Resentment of the labour laws was among the grievances behind the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

titles: In 1351, Getting a Pay Rise Was a Crime
Why Medieval Killers Ran to the Church
One Pub Fight, One Death, One Walk to Dover
publishing.description: Harvest, 1351. Three years after the Black Death, workers are scarce, and taking a pay rise is against the law. After fourteen hours of hard yakka, your best mate flashes his illegal wage in the alehouse, someone threatens to dob him in, and a jug comes down. Then the real horror starts: no police, a whole village forced to hunt one of its own, forty nights of sanctuary, a coroner's inquest where even the jug has to be paid for, and a long walk to Dover with nothing but a wooden cross.
publishing.whats_real: What's real: the 1351 Statute of Labourers and its wage limits, excess pay going to the village's tax, the hue and cry, the coroner's inquest, deodands, sanctuary and abjuring the realm (including a 1353 case with 12 days to reach Dover) are documented (sources below). You, Jacko, Simmo, Maud and the coroner are fictional, and the Aussie slang is ours, not 1351's.
